variants.title: Budget the series
variants.context: Active series = targets × post-relabel series per target. Samples per second = active series ÷ scrape interval. Raw local-block estimate = samples per second × retention seconds × bytes per sample (about 1–2). Provisioned disk = raw estimate ÷ (1 − reserved headroom).
variants.prompt: 200 targets each expose 1,500 series after relabeling. How many active series is that?

variants.title: Budget the series
variants.context: Active series = targets × post-relabel series per target. Samples per second = active series ÷ scrape interval. Raw local-block estimate = samples per second × retention seconds × bytes per sample (about 1–2). Provisioned disk = raw estimate ÷ (1 − reserved headroom).
variants.prompt: 300,000 active series are scraped every 15 seconds. How many samples per second?
variants.hint: Divide series by the scrape interval in seconds.

mistakes.feedback: Divide by the interval, do not multiply.
Each series produces a sample every 15 seconds, not every second.

variants.title: Budget the series
variants.context: Active series = targets × post-relabel series per target. Samples per second = active series ÷ scrape interval. Raw local-block estimate = samples per second × retention seconds × bytes per sample (about 1–2). Provisioned disk = raw estimate ÷ (1 − reserved headroom).
variants.prompt: The raw local-block estimate is 40 GB and you reserve 20% headroom. How much disk should be provisioned?
variants.explanation: 40 ÷ 0.8 = 50 GB, so retained blocks stay below the full disk and cleanup can run.

mistakes.feedback: Headroom means raw is 80% of the disk, not 120% of raw.
That leaves no room for cleanup or the WAL.

variants.title: Pick the metric type
variants.context: Counter: cumulative total, query with rate() or increase(). Gauge: current value that moves up and down. Histogram: aggregatable buckets, count, and sum. Summary: client-side quantiles that generally cannot be aggregated across instances.
variants.prompt: Total HTTP requests handled since process start. Which type, and how should it be queried?
options: A counter, queried with rate() over a range.
A gauge, alerting on the raw value.
optionFeedback: Counters only increase; rate() handles resets.
The raw total keeps growing; it is not a level.
Summaries are for quantiles.
variants.hint: Does the value ever go down?
variants.explanation: Never alert on a raw counter total.

variants.title: Pick the metric type
variants.context: Counter: cumulative total, query with rate() or increase(). Gauge: current value that moves up and down. Histogram: aggregatable buckets, count, and sum. Summary: client-side quantiles that generally cannot be aggregated across instances.
variants.prompt: Current queue depth that rises and falls. Which type?
optionFeedback: Gauges represent a current value.
Counters cannot decrease.
Histograms record distributions.
variants.explanation: Do not apply counter-reset logic to a gauge.

variants.title: Pick the metric type
variants.context: Counter: cumulative total, query with rate() or increase(). Gauge: current value that moves up and down. Histogram: aggregatable buckets, count, and sum. Summary: client-side quantiles that generally cannot be aggregated across instances.
variants.prompt: You need p95 latency aggregated across all instances. Which type?
options: A histogram, whose buckets can be aggregated before computing the quantile.
A gauge of the last latency.
optionFeedback: Bucket counts add across instances; quantiles do not.
Client-side quantiles generally cannot be aggregated across instances.
A single last value is not a distribution.
variants.explanation: Bucket boundaries determine both cost and which questions can be answered.

variants.title: Choose labels
variants.context: Every unique metric name and label set is a separate series. Keep bounded dimensions; aggregate raw URL paths into route templates; avoid user IDs, request IDs, and timestamps as labels.
variants.prompt: A metric carries a request_id label. What happens?
options: Nearly every request creates a new series; the cardinality explodes.
optionFeedback: Every unique label set is a separate series.
Series cost memory and disk.
More series slow queries.
variants.hint: How many distinct values will this label have?

variants.title: Choose labels
variants.context: Every unique metric name and label set is a separate series. Keep bounded dimensions; aggregate raw URL paths into route templates; avoid user IDs, request IDs, and timestamps as labels.
variants.prompt: URL paths such as /users/12345 are used as a label value. What is the fix?
options: Aggregate raw paths into route templates such as /users/{id} before exporting.
optionFeedback: Templates keep the dimension bounded and useful.
Route is a valuable bounded dimension.
Hashing keeps the cardinality.
variants.hint: Which form is bounded and still meaningful?
variants.explanation: Keep bounded dimensions such as method, route template, and status class.

variants.title: Choose labels
variants.context: Every unique metric name and label set is a separate series. Keep bounded dimensions; aggregate raw URL paths into route templates; avoid user IDs, request IDs, and timestamps as labels.
variants.prompt: Metric relabeling drops half the series before ingestion. Which count should the budget use?
optionFeedback: Only ingested series cost storage and memory.
Dropped series never become samples.
Targets are one factor; series per target is the other.
variants.hint: Which series actually reach the TSDB?

variants.title: Read the failure
variants.context: A target failure records up as 0. A slow rule group misses evaluations while scraping stays healthy. An Alertmanager outage interrupts notification delivery, not alert state. A remote-write outage grows a queue and can lose data after the WAL window. The local TSDB is not clustered.
variants.prompt: Alertmanager is down. What happens to an alert whose PromQL condition is true?
options: Prometheus still holds the alert state; grouping and notification delivery are interrupted.
optionFeedback: Alertmanager does not evaluate PromQL.
State lives in Prometheus.
Rule evaluation continues.
variants.hint: Who evaluates the rule, and who notifies?
variants.explanation: Trace collection, rules, alerts, and remote write separately.

variants.title: Read the failure
variants.context: A target failure records up as 0. A slow rule group misses evaluations while scraping stays healthy. An Alertmanager outage interrupts notification delivery, not alert state. A remote-write outage grows a queue and can lose data after the WAL window. The local TSDB is not clustered.
variants.prompt: Remote write to long-term storage fails for hours. What is the risk?
options: The queue grows and unsent data can be lost after the WAL window is compacted.
optionFeedback: The WAL bounds how long unsent samples survive.
Retries are bounded by the WAL window.
Local ingestion continues.
variants.explanation: Remote write does not replace the local TSDB.

variants.title: Read the failure
variants.context: A target failure records up as 0. A slow rule group misses evaluations while scraping stays healthy. An Alertmanager outage interrupts notification delivery, not alert state. A remote-write outage grows a queue and can lose data after the WAL window. The local TSDB is not clustered.
variants.prompt: A target’s scrape fails. What does Prometheus record?
optionFeedback: up is the scrape health series.
The failure is recorded explicitly.
Missing samples are not zeros.
variants.explanation: Decide whether missing data means silence, discovery failure, or scrape failure before paging.

variants.title: Write correct PromQL
variants.context: Apply rate() to counters over a range with enough samples; aggregate numerator and denominator over compatible labels before dividing; use histogram_quantile() on aggregated bucket rates keeping le; decide what missing data means before paging.
variants.prompt: An error ratio divides errors by requests with different label sets and returns nothing. What is wrong?
options: Aggregate the numerator and denominator over compatible labels before dividing.
optionFeedback: Vector matching needs compatible labels.
Range does not fix label mismatch.
Metric type is not the issue.
variants.hint: Which labels must match for the division?
variants.explanation: Preserve only the dimensions the dashboard needs.

variants.title: Write correct PromQL
variants.context: Apply rate() to counters over a range with enough samples; aggregate numerator and denominator over compatible labels before dividing; use histogram_quantile() on aggregated bucket rates keeping le; decide what missing data means before paging.
variants.prompt: histogram_quantile returns NaN after summing buckets without le. What is missing?
options: Keep the le label when aggregating bucket rates.
optionFeedback: Bucket boundaries live in le.
Quantile value is not the issue.
Summaries cannot be aggregated this way.
variants.hint: Which label encodes the bucket boundary?
variants.explanation: Use histogram_quantile() on aggregated bucket rates and retain le.

variants.title: Write correct PromQL
variants.context: Apply rate() to counters over a range with enough samples; aggregate numerator and denominator over compatible labels before dividing; use histogram_quantile() on aggregated bucket rates keeping le; decide what missing data means before paging.
variants.prompt: rate(http_requests_total[15s]) with a 15-second scrape interval returns gaps. Why?
options: The range must contain enough samples; use a range spanning several scrapes.
optionFeedback: A range equal to one interval often holds one sample or none.
rate() is for counters.
Resets are handled by rate().
variants.hint: How many samples fall in the range?
variants.explanation: Choose a range that contains enough samples for the scrape interval.
